title: Solve Area Problems
goal: I can solve real-world area problems: find the facts, draw or use a picture, write an equation, and label the answer.
catchAll: Read, find the numbers, picture the shape, write an equation, solve, and label the answer with square units.

teacher.def: number of unit squares needed to cover the INSIDE of a shape or region
a square that is 1 unit tall and 1 unit wide
to find the area of a rectangle, you multiply the length and the width

glossary.equation: a number sentence with an equals sign, like 6 × 4 = 24
glossary.label: write the unit with the answer, like 24 square feet

screens.title: A plan for area problems
text: 1. Read the problem. 2. Find the numbers you need. 3. Look at or draw the shape.
4. Write an equation. 5. Solve. 6. Label the answer. 7. Check that it makes sense.

screens.title: A rectangle problem
text: A banner is 15 feet long and 4 feet wide. What is its area?
Equation: 15 × 4. Split 15 into 10 + 5: 40 + 20 = 60. The banner covers 60 square feet.

item.prompt: A classroom rug is 6 feet long and 5 feet wide. Which equation finds its area?

options.why: Adding the sides does not find area.
That measures all the way around the rug, not the space it covers.

item.yes: Yes! The rug covers 30 square feet.

screens.title: A shape made of parts
text: A garden has this shape. Split it into rectangles: 5 by 1, 2 by 2 and 5 by 2.
screens.caption: Three parts: 5 + 4 + 10 = 19

screens.title: Compare areas
text: A garden 4 yards by 4 yards covers 16 square yards. One 3 yards by 5 yards covers 15 square yards.
16 is more than 15, so the square garden is bigger, even though it is not longer.

screens.title: Area is not the edge
text: Some problems ask how much is covered: that is area, in square units.
Adding up the sides measures around the outside. That is a different kind of problem.

item.prompt: A poster is 7 feet long and 3 feet wide. It covers 3 × 7 = 21 of what?

options.why: A length is in feet. What the poster covers is in square feet.
The number tells how much space one poster covers.

item.yes: Yes! Area is labeled in square units.

screens.title: Explain My Thinking: does my answer make sense?

item.prompt: How do you know your answer to an area problem makes sense? Write your answer in a sentence.
hints: Compare your answer with a simple rectangle that the figure fits inside. Did you write the unit?
item.example: I know my answer makes sense because I can compare it with a shape I know, and I labeled the area in square units.
show: Write one sentence that answers the question.
Here is one way to say it: I know my answer makes sense because I can compare it with a shape I know, and I labeled the area in square units.

watch.takeaway: Find the numbers, picture the shape, write an equation, solve, and label the answer in square units. Then check it makes sense.

examples.title: Example A: a garden with three parts

steps.say: 1. Read: a city garden has this shape. What is its area?
2. Find the facts: the sides are in meters, and the garden is not one rectangle.
3. Choose a model: split it into three rectangles, 5 by 1, 2 by 2 and 5 by 2.
4. Write the equation: multiply each part, then add.
5. Calculate: 5 + 4 + 10.
6. Label the answer: 19 square meters.
7. Check: the garden fits inside a 5 by 5 square (25), and 19 is less than 25. It makes sense.

options.text: It is less than the 5 by 5 square (25) the garden fits inside.

options.why: Odd does not matter. Compare with a shape you know.
The number of parts does not check the answer.

why.yes: Yes! Comparing with a simple shape is a good check.

examples.title: Example B: which garden is bigger?

steps.say: Problem: Ray's garden is 4 yards by 4 yards. Bo's garden is 5 yards by 3 yards. Whose garden has a greater area?
Step 1: Ray's garden.
Step 2: Bo's garden.
Step 3: Compare: 16 is more than 15.
Step 4: Ray's garden has the greater area, 16 square yards.
1. Read: a poster is 7 feet long and 3 feet wide. It is made 10 feet long. How much more area does it cover?
2. Find the facts: old poster 7 by 3 feet; new poster 10 by 3 feet.
3. Choose a model: the new poster is the old one plus a 3 by 3 part.
4. Write the equations: the old area and the new area.
5. Calculate: the new area, then the difference.
6. Label the answer: 9 more square feet.
7. Check: the added part is 3 by 3, and 3 × 3 = 9. It matches.

examples.title: Example D: turf for a baseball training area

steps.say: 1. Read the problem: a school is putting turf on the floor of a baseball training area. The floor has this shape. How many square feet of turf does it need?
2. Find the information we need: 12 feet and 6 feet for the big part, and 5 feet and 4 feet for the small part. The sides are in feet, so the answer is in square feet.
3. Understand the shape: the floor is not one rectangle. It is a wide top part with a smaller part joined below it, like an L.
4. Choose a strategy: draw a line to split the floor into two rectangles with no overlap. The top part is 12 by 6. The bottom part is 5 by 4.
5. Write an equation for each part. Top: 12 × 6 = 72. Bottom: 5 × 4 = 20.
6. Calculate: add the two partial areas, 72 + 20. Label the answer in square units: 92 square feet.

7. Explain and check: the two rectangles cover the whole floor with no gaps and no overlap, so adding their areas gives the area of the whole floor. The floor fits inside a 12 by 10 rectangle, which is 120 square feet, and 92 is less than 120. The answer makes sense.

why.prompt: Why can we add 72 and 20 to find the area of the whole floor?

options.text: The two rectangles cover the whole floor with no gaps and no overlap.
Because we always add to find area.
options.why: Each rectangle's area comes from multiplying. We add only because the floor is split into parts.
The size of the numbers does not decide it. What matters is that the parts cover the floor with no overlap.

why.yes: Yes! The parts cover the floor exactly once, so their areas add up to the whole.

items.prompt: Dana found the area of this classroom floor by multiplying the longest length by the longest width: 10 × 8 = 80 square feet. What went wrong?

options.text: She treated the floor as one big rectangle, but part of that rectangle is empty.
She added the length and the width.
options.why: She multiplied, and 10 × 8 = 80 is a true product. The problem is that the floor does not fill a 10 by 8 rectangle.

options.text: She should have used the shortest sides.
options.why: The shortest sides do not give the area either. Split the floor into rectangles and add their areas.
80 square feet is more than the floor covers. The floor has an empty corner.

hints: Does the floor fill the whole 10 by 8 rectangle? Look at the empty corner.
show: The floor is two rectangles: 10 × 3 = 30 and 4 × 5 = 20.
80 is too big because it counts the empty corner.
items.yes: Yes! The empty corner was counted. The real area is 50 square feet.

sections.heading: What your child is learning
sections.text: Your child solves real-world area problems: finding the numbers, using or drawing a picture, writing an equation, solving, labeling the answer in square units, and checking it makes sense.

Plan a garden on graph paper: two beds, which covers more?

list: Adding the sides (that measures around the outside) when the question asks what is covered.
Forgetting a part of a composite shape.
